upstream.sha_note: master HEAD, which is v0.7.2 (7708026) plus TWO unreleased scanner commits, pinned deliberately rather than pinning the tag. 4463985d 'handle multiline strings without indent' is a real parse fix; a1c4812a replaces `#define SCN_SUCC/STOP/FAIL` with a `ScanStatus` enum, which matters because three scanner functions returned `char` while SCN_FAIL is -1 — on any target where char is unsigned that comparison is broken, so it is a portability fix and not a cosmetic one. MEASURED: the two commits change 0 of 3217 corpus verdicts on this box (both shas: 3114 clean, 103 ERROR, identical file sets, and `src/parser.c` is byte-identical because both commits touch only the hand-written scanner). They are pinned anyway because the corpus does not contain the construct #36 fixes and this box's char is signed; the ledger says so rather than implying the pin was free.
upstream.version_note: 0.7.2 is what upstream's own Cargo.toml, package.json and tree-sitter.json metadata all say at this sha; upstream has not cut a release for the two commits above.

upstream_choice.summary: tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-yaml, the maintained fork — NOT ikatyang/tree-sitter-yaml, which has more stars and is the one npm still points at.
upstream_choice.evidence: ikatyang/tree-sitter-yaml: 120 stars, 33 open issues, default-branch HEAD 2021-05-11 (5.3 years), and that last commit is a dependabot bump rather than a grammar change. tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-yaml: 56 stars, 16 open issues, default-branch HEAD 2026-05-22, and that commit is a scanner fix. crates.io's `tree-sitter-yaml` (3.45 M downloads all-time, 1.58 M recent — the roadmap's 3.4 M) resolves to the fork; npm's `tree-sitter-yaml` (243 K/month — the roadmap's 246 K) still resolves to ikatyang. So ROADMAP's two popularity figures for 'yaml' are measuring two different grammars, one of them five years dead.
upstream_choice.method_note: Chosen on default-branch HEAD, not on GitHub's `pushed_at`, and not on stars. `pushed_at` counts any branch: it reports ikatyang as last pushed 2023-11-05, understating the staleness of the code anyone would actually get by 2.5 years. ROADMAP section 3's stale-grammar table is built on `pushed_at` and inherits that error wherever a repo has a live side branch and a dead default branch. Credit to the parallel tbtoml session, which hit the same thing on tree-sitter-toml (395 days by `pushed_at`, 617 on master).

patches.title: row counters overflow past line 32768
patches.origin: treebank; the row overflow this ledger's `the_one_gap` diagnosed on prometheus's 40,011-line rules_large.yml and left unfixed. The ranked-corpus sweep then produced it as ALL FOUR of its gap files (corpus/yaml/reports/REPORT.md booked them as three clusters, because the wrap lands at a different construct in each file, but the root cause is one). Tracked at https://github.com/PowderworksCode/treebank/issues/58 and raised upstream at https://github.com/tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-yaml/issues/49; the patch applies directly to the pinned sha and touches no other patch.

evidence.repro: a: 1\n + 32767 EMPTY LINES + b: 2\n  (32,777 bytes; `b` sits on row 32768, the first row an int16_t cannot hold). Written out rather than inlined because the literal is 32,769 lines long.
evidence.repro_note: The blank lines are filler and 1 byte each, so this is the SMALLEST possible repro for a row-32768 bug: any such file has to reach row 32768, and no row can be shorter than its newline. Bisected exactly — 32766 blank lines parse clean, 32767 do not, and 2**15 = 32768. Content, not bytes: a 200 KB single-line file parses clean, and so do 40,000 blank lines with nothing after them.  Confirmed valid by this ledger's oracle (js-yaml 5.2.3 parseEvents), as are all four corpus gap files.
evidence.diagnosis: NOT a YAML construct — an integer overflow in the hand-written scanner. `src/scanner.c` kept its row state in `int16_t` (`row`, `blk_imp_row`, and the temporaries `cur_row`/`end_row`, plus the `bgn_row` local that feeds `blk_imp_row`). At row 32768 `row` wraps negative; `blk_imp_row != bgn_row` — the test that decides whether a block-implicit key starts a new mapping — then compares a wrapped row against an unwrapped one, every indentation decision after that point is wrong, and the remainder of the file collapses into a single ERROR node spanning back to [0,0]. The fix widens exactly those five to `int32_t` and nothing else. Serialization: the two persistent int32 fields are written FIRST, so the header is 4+4+2+2+2 = 14 bytes with every field naturally aligned (it was 10 bytes, all int16), and the indent stacks that follow are untouched, so the number of indent levels that fit in TREE_SITTER_SERIALIZATION_BUFFER_SIZE is unchanged. Columns are deliberately NOT widened — see remaining_gaps_note.

first_seen.note: 72,060 lines. The other three gap files are 49,299 / 49,054 / 35,649 lines — argoproj.io_workflows.yaml, kserve-crds.yaml and a second copy of the kuberay manifest set. Generated Kubernetes CRD bundles, exactly the population predicted when the bug was first diagnosed on a prometheus rules file.

evidence.evidence_note: Four files, and they are every gap file in the corpus: the sweep goes to ZERO gaps, with the single remaining failure the ooapiv6.yaml noise file the oracle also rejects. Both numbers were measured over the identical 26,628-file corpus with only this patch reverted and restored, so they are the same experiment with one variable changed. Zero regressions: upstream's own corpus tests go 131/131 to 132/132 (the new case is the 132nd), the 25 syntax-highlighting assertions are unchanged, and the negative corpus is still fully rejected. The corpus test is verified to FAIL on the pinned sha and pass with the patch — checked by reverting src/scanner.c alone, regenerating and re-running `tree-sitter test`, rather than assumed from the sweep.
evidence.test_size_note: The corpus test is 32,769 lines and the patch is 69 KB, of which 32,767 lines are the blank filler. That is the irreducible cost of a regression test for a bug whose trigger IS a line number, and it is stated here because the size looks like a mistake and is not. The alternative — no test, and rely on the sweep's four 35k-72k-line CRD bundles — was rejected: those files live in a gitignored corpus that is refetched, so nothing in the committed tree would hold the grammar to this fix.
evidence.remaining_gaps_note: COLUMNS ARE STILL int16_t, on purpose. `col`, `blk_imp_col`, `blk_imp_tab` and both indent stacks hold columns, and a line past column 32767 would wrap the same way. It is not fixed here because (a) no file in the 26,628-file corpus or the 3,217-file measurement corpus demonstrates it — a 200 KB single-line file parses clean — and (b) fixing it properly means widening the two indent STACKS, which are serialized per indent level against a fixed TREE_SITTER_SERIALIZATION_BUFFER_SIZE, so it would halve the nesting depth the scanner can round-trip. That is a real trade to make against evidence, and there is none yet. Widening the columns without the stacks would be worse than either: `push_ind` stores a column, so the truncation would just move.
evidence.upstream_status: reported upstream as tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-yaml#49; no fix upstream at the pinned sha. Retire this patch if it merges.

patches.title: at most one %YAML directive per document
patches.origin: treebank; found by scoring the grammar against yaml/yaml-test-suite data-2022-01-17 rather than by a corpus sweep, which cannot see this direction at all. Not reported upstream.

evidence.diagnosis: `_drs_doc` was `seq(repeat1($._s_dir), $._exp_doc)` with `_s_dir` a plain choice of the three directive kinds, so any number of %YAML directives parsed. YAML 1.2.2 6.8.1 allows AT MOST ONE per document, while %TAG and reserved directives may repeat and may sit on either side of it — which is a regular language, so the fix is a restructured choice (`repeat(other) yaml repeat(other) | repeat1(other)`) and needs no new state. THE GRAMMAR CHANGE ALONE IS A REGRESSION, which is why this patch also touches the scanner: the '%' branch of the scanner's dispatch was gated on `valid_symbols[S_DIR_YML_BGN]` alone, even though `scn_dir_bgn` decides between all three directive-start symbols by reading the name. Once the grammar stopped accepting a second %YAML, that gate went false and the scanner went blind to '%' ENTIRELY, so a %TAG following a %YAML stopped scanning. The gate now admits any of the three. Caught by the new corpus test, which is a %YAML followed by two %TAG directives.

first_seen.note: Not a corpus file. No file in the 26,636-file ranked corpus carries a duplicate %YAML directive, which is why the sweep is silent on this patch and the suite is not.

evidence.evidence_note: Moves ZERO corpus files by design — this patch exists to stop the grammar accepting something invalid, and the corpus contains no instance. The number that moves is the suite's accepts-invalid, 6 -> 5, with rejects-valid still 0 across all 308 expect-valid cases. Corpus tests 132 -> 133.

patches.title: deficient indentation in multi-line double-quoted scalars
patches.origin: treebank; found against yaml-test-suite. It narrows a condition introduced by upstream commit 4463985d ('handle multiline strings without indent'), one of the two unreleased scanner commits this ledger pins deliberately — see `upstream.sha_note`. Not reported upstream.

evidence.repro:
---
quoted: "a
b
c"
  (suite case QB6E); and foo: "bar
<TAB>baz"
 (suite case DK95/01) — ONE defect, two cases.
evidence.diagnosis: The BR_DQT_STR_CTN branch of the scanner's dispatch read `(is_br || has_nwl)`. `is_br` is the real test — `has_nwl && leading_spaces > cur_ind` — and `|| has_nwl` waives it, so a continuation line of a multi-line double-quoted scalar was accepted at ANY indentation, including column 0 under a block mapping key and including a line indented with a TAB (`leading_spaces` stops counting at the first tab, so a tab-indented line has `leading_spaces == 0`). js-yaml calls both 'deficient indentation'. Dropping the `|| has_nwl` fixes both. The construct upstream added it for still works and is covered: at the DOCUMENT ROOT the required indent is -1 in this scanner's convention, so `is_br` is already true and an unindented multi-line scalar scans without the waiver — verified for the folded form, the escaped-newline form, inside a sequence item, and nested under a key.
evidence.upstream_test_note: THIS PATCH REWRITES ONE OF UPSTREAM'S OWN CORPUS TESTS, which is a divergence worth stating plainly rather than burying in the diff. `test/corpus/99_issues.txt`'s 'Double-quote newline escape (#10)' asserts that `root: "a\\<nl>b\\<nl>c"` parses clean. MEASURED against this ledger's oracle: that input is INVALID ('deficient indentation'), and the same text with one leading space on each continuation is valid. So the upstream test asserts a document that is not YAML. It is replaced by two tests that keep the issue's intent — the same escaped-newline construct unindented AT THE ROOT, where it is genuinely valid, and the indented-under-a-key form — rather than deleted. Expect a conflict here on any upstream bump that touches that file.

first_seen.note: Not a corpus file, and the near miss is worth recording: this ledger's `sweep.ranked_corpus.what_the_oracle_choice_costs` describes 6 real corpus files of a RELATED deficient-indentation class — multi-line flow COLLECTIONS whose closing bracket sits in the key's column, which libyaml and go-yaml accept and js-yaml rejects. Those are a different production and this patch deliberately does not touch them; the sweep confirms it, moving 0 files.

evidence.evidence_note: Two suite cases for one condition, 5 -> 3, and rejects-valid stays 0 over all 308 expect-valid cases — which is the check that matters here, because waiving an indentation rule is the kind of change that buys accepts-invalid at the cost of rejects-valid. Zero corpus movement. Corpus tests 133 -> 134.

patches.title: tab used as block scalar indentation
patches.origin: treebank; found against yaml-test-suite. Not reported upstream.

evidence.diagnosis: `scn_blk_str_bgn`'s auto-detection loop only advances over ' ', so a TAB fell into the branch that treats the character as the start of content. With the tab at column 0 under a mapping at indent 0 the detected indentation came out equal to the parent's, the block scalar was emitted empty, and the tab line was then swallowed by the generic whitespace skip — the tab appeared in NO node at all. js-yaml: 'tab characters must not be used in indentation'. The fix rejects the block scalar start when the detection line begins with a tab that is still inside the parent's indentation.
evidence.boundary_note: THE BOUND IS STRICT (`< cur_ind`) AND THE OFF-BY-ONE IS THE WHOLE PATCH. The suite contains the adjacent valid case: Y79Y/001 is byte-for-byte Y79Y/000 with ONE LEADING SPACE, and it is valid, because that space puts the tab past the parent's indentation where it is ordinary content. Written first as `<= cur_ind`, which scored 4 rejects-valid — 96NN/00, 96NN/01, R4YG and Y79Y/001, every one of them a tab sitting one column past the parent. Recorded because the suite is the only thing that catches it: the corpus contains no instance in either direction.
evidence.evidence_note: 3 -> 2 accepts-invalid, 0 rejects-valid, zero corpus movement. The new corpus test is the VALID neighbour (`foo: |-` then one space and a tab), not the invalid case, because the invalid case lives in test/negative and the thing most likely to break later is the boundary. Corpus tests 134 -> 135.

patches.title: leading empty line deeper than the block scalar's content
patches.origin: treebank; found against yaml-test-suite and then found to occur in the ranked corpus. Not reported upstream.

evidence.repro:
empty block scalar: >
<SP>
<SP><SP>
<SP><SP><SP>
<SP># comment
  (suite case S98Z)
evidence.diagnosis: YAML 1.2.2 8.1.1.1: it is an error for any of a block scalar's leading empty lines to contain more spaces than its first non-empty line, because the auto-detected indentation would then be taken from whitespace rather than from content. `scn_blk_str_bgn` raised its running `ind` from every empty line and never compared it against the first content line. The fix tracks the deepest leading empty line separately (`max_bl_ind`) and rejects the block scalar start when it exceeds the first non-empty line's indentation. The sentinel is -2, below every real column, so a scalar with NO leading empty lines and one that reaches EOF before any content are both untouched — the two cases a naive comparison against `ind` would break, since `ind` starts at the parent's indentation.

battery.what: 9 hand-built block-scalar cases spanning the boundary, each checked against the oracle before the fix was written and against the grammar after
battery.cases: no-blank/content; blank-then-key; blank2-then-content1; blank1-then-content2; blank2-then-content2; S98Z; blank3-then-content1; no-blank-content2; blank-only-then-EOF
battery.why: The rule has two edges — 'more spaces than the first non-empty line' and 'only if there IS a leading empty line' — and the suite exercises one case. Deriving the predicate from a battery first is what kept `foo: >` followed by `bar: 1` (valid, and the shape an empty block scalar actually takes in real YAML) from being rejected.

first_seen.note: Line 50 is `    values: |-`, followed by a SIX-space empty line and then content at indent 4. Found by the sweep after the fix, not before — it was one of the seven corpus files the oracle rejects and the grammar accepted.

evidence.sweep_direction_note: THE PASS COUNT GOES DOWN BY ONE AND THAT IS THE POINT, which is worth spelling out because every other patch in this repo is judged by the pass count going UP. The file that stops passing is the params.yml above; this ledger's oracle independently rejects it for the same reason js-yaml gives for S98Z ('bad indentation of a mapping entry'), so it is booked as NOISE, `gap_files` stays 0, and the grammar's accepts-invalid over the real corpus goes 6 -> 5. scripts/check.sh gates on `passed > PASS_BEFORE`, which is the right gate for a gap-closing patch and the WRONG SHAPE for an accepts-invalid one: a patch that correctly starts rejecting invalid files can only lower that number. Read the gap/noise split, not the pass count, when judging a patch of this kind.
evidence.evidence_note: 2 -> 1 accepts-invalid on the suite and 6 -> 5 on the real corpus, with rejects-valid still 0. Corpus tests 135 -> 137; the two new ones are both VALID neighbours (a leading empty line no deeper than the content, and an empty block scalar followed by the next key), for the same reason as 0006.

oracle.tool: tools/yaml-oracle/check.mjs (js-yaml `parseEvents` behind an explicit YAML 1.2.2 section 5.2 decode layer), driven through lang::stdin_oracle::run_node
oracle.dialect: YAML 1.2 as js-yaml 5.2 implements it, at the parse stage
oracle.stage: parse (event stream) — before composition, tag resolution and construction
oracle.authority_note: THIS IS THE FIRST GRAMMAR WHOSE ORACLE IS A CHOICE RATHER THAN A FACT, and `authority` exists to say so in one word. Every other language has a parser everyone appeals to: rust has syn, python has CPython, php has `php -l`, lua has PUC-Rio, zig has std.zig.Ast, and for those `authority` is "reference" (the default) and `position` is absent. YAML has no such implementation. Measured, not assumed: over the official conformance suite the four mainstream parsers score 83.3% (libyaml), 81.8% (go-yaml v3), 99.3% (eemeli `yaml`) and 100% (js-yaml), and they disagree with EACH OTHER on 67 of 402 cases — an order of magnitude past the 6.86% version spread that treebank-zig calls the most load-bearing field it has. Every verdict this grammar's sweep records is relative to the tool named above, and a gap number quoted without it is not a claim this ledger makes.

considered.tool: libyaml 0.2.5 via PyYAML 6.0.1's CParser, `yaml.parse` event stream
considered.why_not: THE RUNNER-UP, and the one ROADMAP names for this language. It wins the battery outright — 0 of 21 wrong, against the chosen oracle's 1 — and it is 0.14 s/1000 against 0.13. It loses on the column that decides gap accounting: 51 of the suite's 308 valid cases are rejected, against 0. `validate()` runs only on files the grammar already failed, so each of those 51 would be booked as corpus NOISE and would hide a grammar gap. libyaml's rejects are not exotic — they include tabs in literals, zero-indented block scalars, empty keys, `%YAML` reserved directives, anchors containing a colon, and eight of the specification's own examples. It also rejects a bare document after a `...` end marker, which the suite calls valid (7Z25) and which occurs in the real corpus (helm's msgblock.yaml), so this is not only a hard-tail phenomenon.
considered.also_measured: PyYAML's version is a BINDING version and says nothing about the parser: the parser is libyaml, whose version had to be read from the C library (`_yaml.get_version_string()` -> 0.2.5) and is invisible to pip. Any ledger citing a parser or a spec from a package version string is citing the wrong thing.

considered.why_not: THE STAGE IS A BIGGER LEVER THAN THE PARSER FOR THIS LANGUAGE, which is the opposite of what the roadmap's framing suggests, and it is why `stage` is a field. Same parser, same version, different stage: 73 of 3217 real corpus verdicts flip (2.27%) where libyaml-vs-go-yaml at the same stage flip 0. The 73 are unresolvable tags (ansible's `!vault`) and duplicate keys. Neither is a syntax property and a tree-sitter grammar cannot see either, so a load-stage oracle would call files invalid for reasons the grammar is not responsible for and hide real gaps behind them. Same shape as ROADMAP section 9's python finding, where `ast.parse` vs `compile(..., 'exec')` moved 11 of 30 supposed gaps — measured here at 2.27% rather than assumed.

Lowest conformance of the four (81.8%), 58 rejects-valid, and 1.5x the cost. It also failed the I/O honesty check in a way worth recording because the repo has not met this direction before: Go's `os.Open` SUCCEEDS on a directory, so the read error arrives later as a decode error and the driver books a directory as `invalid` — a verdict, not a failure. `exec_oracle`'s `reject_statuses` design cannot catch that, because the tool is answering, just about the wrong thing. The parallel tbtoml session found the same defect class with the opposite polarity in taplo (`taplo lint` on a path matching nothing exits 0, i.e. valid, which manufactures phantom gaps and dispatches fix agents at files that do not exist). An oracle's `unreadable_note` should therefore say WHICH DIRECTION the tool fails in, not merely that it was handled.

DISQUALIFIED ON THE BATTERY, not on its conformance, which is 99.3% and second-best. It performs no control-character validation at all: NUL, form feed, DEL and a raw ESC are all accepted, as is ill-formed UTF-8 — 8 of 21 battery cases wrong, every one of them in the gap-MANUFACTURING direction. That matters more than it sounds: treebank-lua established that tree-sitter's lexer reserves codepoint 0 for EOF, so a NUL anywhere truncates the parse and the remainder becomes ERROR — a failure no grammar.js change can fix. An oracle that calls those files valid turns each into a phantom gap and spends a fix agent on it. This candidate was still the front-runner on conformance alone when the battery was run; it is the cleanest evidence either grammar has that A CONFORMANCE SCORE IS NOT A SAFETY PROPERTY. It is also 6x the cost (0.77 s/1000, 2.4 MB/s).

ZERO REJECTION POWER: it accepts all 94 of the suite's expected-error cases, because the CST parser is error-tolerant by design and reports problems on the composed Document instead. An oracle that calls everything valid makes every grammar failure a gap. This is exactly the failure ROADMAP #13 predicts for CSS, met here by accident on a different language, and it is the reason a candidate must be scored against expected-ERROR cases and not against agreement with other parsers.

considered.tool: js-yaml 5.2.3 `loadAll` (the chosen parser, at the load stage)
considered.why_not: 32 rejects-valid against `parseEvents`'s 0, for the same reason libyaml's load stage loses: schema resolution and construction reject documents whose SYNTAX is fine. Recorded so the stage choice inside the chosen tool is visible as a measured decision rather than a default.

NOT A DIFFERENT PARSER — the same parser with the decode layer left implicit, kept in this list because it is what a reasonable implementation looks like and it is wrong. `readFileSync(path,'utf8')` substitutes U+FFFD for ill-formed UTF-8 (so ill-formed bytes parse as valid YAML), mojibakes UTF-16 (so both UTF-16 cases are rejected), and leaves a leading BOM in the string, which js-yaml counts as content: `"\uFEFFa: 1\nb: 2\n"` is rejected with "end of the stream or a document separator is expected (2:1)" where libyaml, go-yaml and eemeli all accept it and 1.2.2 section 5.2 permits it. That single defect caused 12 of the corpus disagreements, all of them helm's `frobnitz_with_bom` fixtures, all gap-hiding. ZERO of the suite's 402 cases begin with a BOM, so 402/402 cannot see it.

position.why_this_one: Chosen on measured conformance to the community's own arbiter, then checked against a population that arbiter is blind to. js-yaml 5.2.3's event parser is the only candidate that scores 402/402 on yaml-test-suite with 0 accepts-invalid AND 0 rejects-valid, and rejects-valid is the direction that hides grammar gaps. With the section 5.2 decode layer supplied it is also 20 of 21 on the encoding battery, within 3 files of libyaml on 3217 real files, and the cheapest of the four (0.13 s/1000, 17 MB/s).
position.verdicts_are_relative_to: js-yaml 5.2.3's event parser at the parse stage, with this repo's decode layer. Concretely: `invalid` here means "js-yaml 5.2 cannot produce an event stream for these bytes", NOT "this is not YAML" and NOT "libyaml would reject this". On 3 of 3217 real files libyaml disagrees, and on 67 of 402 conformance cases it does. gap_files is an exact count against this oracle and an approximation against any other.
position.basis_and_the_alternative: The basis is spec conformance, because the grammar targets the specification rather than any one implementation. The defensible alternative is deployment weight — libyaml is what actually parses most of the world's YAML (ansible, PyYAML, Ruby, Perl and C bindings all sit on it), so an oracle chosen that way would answer "would the software that reads this file accept it?" instead of "is this YAML?". The two bases differ on 0.09% of real files and 16.7% of conformance cases. This ledger takes the first and records the second, and the disagreement figures above are what a reader needs to convert between them.
position.what_would_change_it: A newer conformance suite that js-yaml has not been tested against would be the strongest evidence either way, and it does not exist: exactly one case has been added to yaml-test-suite since the data-2022-01-17 release (ZYU8), and it carries `skip: true`. So 402/402 is partly a home-field score and cannot currently be checked out of sample against the suite. The encoding battery is the out-of-sample population, and it is where this oracle is weakest and libyaml strongest — that trade is the position.

oracle.note: TWO-VALUED: valid / invalid. Parse-stage only, so no document is constructed, no tag is resolved, no anchor is dereferenced and no duplicate key is diagnosed; a file is judged on its own text with no project context, which for a configuration language means there is nothing to have context about. `check.mjs` refuses to run under any js-yaml major other than 5, following treebank-lua's precedent, because the pinned version IS the dialect and adjudicating with whatever is installed would silently produce verdicts for an unrecorded oracle.
oracle.decode_layer_note: THE DRIVER OWNS PART OF THE SPECIFICATION, and that is a liability, not an implementation detail. js-yaml accepts a JS string, so byte-to-character decoding happens outside the parser: `check.mjs` implements YAML 1.2.2 section 5.2 itself — BOM-based UTF-8/16/32 detection, fatal decoding, and stripping exactly one leading BOM. Measured: with the naive `utf8` read the same parser gets 4 of 21 battery cases wrong; with this layer, 1. libyaml scores 0 without any such layer because it does this in C, so the layer is the price of the conformance win and the ledger states it rather than burying it. One warning for anyone maintaining it: the leading-BOM strip is correct HERE and is not portable advice — the parallel tbtoml session measured that the same strip would break `toml`, which distinguishes leading, doubled and mid-stream BOMs; YAML parsers accept a doubled BOM because U+FEFF is inside `c-printable`, which is why stripping one is verdict-preserving here. Verified, not assumed.
oracle.unreadable_note: AN UNREADABLE FILE IS NOT AN INVALID FILE: the oracle writes the path and reason to stderr and exits 1 rather than emitting a verdict, so a mistyped corpus root fails the sweep instead of booking every grammar failure as noise, driving gap_files to zero and reporting a flawless grammar. A DIRECTORY takes the same path (Node's readFileSync throws EISDIR), which is deliberate and is the case go-yaml's driver got wrong. The DIRECTION of failure is stated on purpose: this oracle fails LOUD. A decode failure, by contrast, is a VERDICT of invalid and not an I/O error, because section 5.2 makes the encoding part of the character stream's well-formedness — the read and the decode are separate try blocks in `check.mjs` for exactly that reason.
oracle.populations_note: Three populations, and each is blind to something the others catch — which is why `disagreement` holds a list rather than one count. corpus: real files, blind to the hard syntax tail (libyaml and go-yaml differ on 0 of 3217 here and on 14 of 402 in the suite) and blind to every control-character case (0 files with a NUL, ill-formed UTF-8, or a lone CR). suite: the community's arbiter, blind to encoding entirely — ZERO of its 402 cases begin with a BOM and none carries a NUL, which is how a 402/402 parser can still mis-reject real BOM'd files. battery: hand-built, so it is blind to whatever its author did not think of, and it is the only population not authored independently of this grammar. The parallel tbtoml session hit the mirror image — toml-test covers BOMs thoroughly while 0 of its 1427 real .toml files carry one — so WHICH population is blind is not predictable per language, and the only way to bound the error is to run all of them. corpus (3217 real .yml/.yaml files, 5.87 MB, from 4 GitHub source archives: ansible 2099, helm 714, prometheus 381, OAI/OpenAPI-Specification 23; mean 1824 B, median 214 B); suite (yaml/yaml-test-suite data-2022-01-17: 402 cases, 308 expect-valid, 94 expect-error); battery (24 hand-built encoding/control cases, 21 decidable from YAML 1.2.2 5.1 c-printable and 5.2 encoding).

cost.measured_on: the ranked corpus: 26,634 files, 74.0 MB, mean 2,780 B, median 458 B
cost.warmup_note: THIS ORACLE HAS TWO FIXED COSTS, NOT ONE, and the earlier figure in this ledger (0.13 s/1000, 17 MB/s) was the second one showing up uncorrected. Process startup is 0.03 s and constant. JIT warm-up is not constant — it is amortised over the batch, and V8 needs roughly 20 MB of input to reach steady state. Measured on slices of this corpus, best of three: 2.0 MB -> 11.6 MB/s, 6.0 MB -> 27.3, 20.0 MB -> 43.6, 40.0 MB -> 44.6, 74.0 MB -> 45.7. The 17 MB/s previously recorded was measured on a 5.87 MB corpus, i.e. inside the warm-up ramp; it understated the oracle's throughput by 2.7x. ROADMAP section 9's method — 'run each oracle with empty stdin to get its startup cost, then subtract' — subtracts only the first fixed cost and is therefore not sufficient for a JIT runtime. This applies to the js, ts and java oracles too, all of which are JIT'd and all of whose published figures were taken at 1000 files.
cost.per_file_vs_per_byte: s/1000 files tracks the corpus's mean FILE SIZE and MB/s tracks warm-up, and the two move independently: a 20 MB slice of 2,330 large files is 0.197 s/1000 at 43.6 MB/s while the full 74 MB of 26,485 files is 0.061 s/1000 at 45.7 MB/s. Quote both, with the corpus's mean and median, or the number means nothing. ROADMAP section 1's Tier A band of 0.2-2 s/1000 is a bytes/second measurement wearing a per-file label; the parallel tbtoml session measured the same effect independently on TOML.

smoke.note: This is the one oracle whose `authority` is `position` rather than `reference`, so the smoke test is asserting that OUR CHOSEN parser still runs and still discriminates — not that YAML has a reference answer. That makes assertion (2) load-bearing here in a way it is not elsewhere: if the js-yaml layer broke into accepting or rejecting everything, no other check in the repository would notice.

corpus.source: GitHub source archives for the top repositories GitHub's own classifier calls YAML, by stars (`github::rank`, the alternative source treebank-bash built).
corpus.ranking: stars, via GitHub's repository search, non-fork and non-archived.
corpus.why_not_debian: YAML is a guest language exactly as shell is — no package is written in it — so `debian::rank`, which ranks popcon by a per-language SLOC floor, is the right shape and is UNUSABLE here for a measured reason: sources.debian.org's SLOC census has no `yaml` category, so the `keep` predicate is identically false and the corpus comes out empty. Checked, not assumed: ansible-core 2.21.2-1, which is YAML by most of its files, reports python=179848, cs=5783, sh=5085, xml=34, makefile=21; prometheus 3.5.3+ds1-3, the source of this grammar's only measured gap, reports yacc=991, sh=465, makefile=243, lex=190. sloccount predates both YAML and Go and counts neither. A second corpus source therefore needs new *data*, not new code.
corpus.ranking_bias: Stars rank repositories people like, not YAML people parse, and a YAML-PRIMARY repository is by construction one whose YAML is the product (chart collections, manifest sets, Actions libraries) rather than one whose YAML is incidental configuration — which is the population Package Room will actually meet. Stated because it is invisible in the number.
corpus.admit_nul: Files containing a NUL are excluded. tree-sitter's lexer reserves codepoint 0 for end-of-input, so a NUL truncates the parse and the remainder becomes ERROR, which no grammar.js change can fix (established by treebank-lua). Measured here: `a: 1\nb: \0\n` parses CLEAN under the grammar while the oracle rejects it, so such a file is silently accepted-invalid rather than a gap or noise; and a NUL inside a quoted scalar is ERROR, so the same byte lands in two different buckets depending on where it sits. Excluding them is the only bucket that is honest.
corpus.admit_templates: Files carrying a bare `{{ … }}` Go template action or a `{% keyword %}` Jinja statement are excluded: a template that renders to YAML is not YAML, and whether it parses is an accident of quoting (`key: {{ .V }}` is two nested flow mappings and fails; `key: "{{ .V }}"` is a quoted scalar and passes). MEASURED on 3217 files: 1031 carry a bare `{{`, and they hold 101 of the 104 files the oracle rejects and 99 of the 103 the grammar fails. Excluding them leaves 2178 files with 3 oracle rejects and 4 grammar failures, and keeps the one real gap. THE COST IS REAL AND IS ~930 FILES: most of those 1031 templates are valid YAML and are dropped anyway. `${{ … }}` is deliberately NOT a marker — GitHub Actions expressions sit inside scalars, and all 32 corpus files whose only `{{` is a `${{` are valid and parse clean. Same rule, same keyword list and same reasoning as treebank-bash's template filter, which was built for gap inflation; here it is corpus hygiene, because these templates are rejected by the oracle rather than accepted by it.
corpus.measurement_corpus: The numbers in this ledger and in ORACLE.md come from a 3217-file, 5.87 MB measurement corpus assembled by hand from four GitHub source archives (ansible 2099, helm 714, prometheus 381, OAI/OpenAPI-Specification 23) before `Lang::rank` existed, so that the oracle could be chosen before anything was vendored. mean 1824 B, median 214 B, p99 13.6 KB, max 1.17 MB. It is NOT the corpus `treebank rank --lang yaml` will build, and the ranked corpus has not been swept yet.

second_source_investigated.question: `ranking_bias` above says GitHub's YAML-primary repositories are YAML-as-product (charts, manifests, Actions libraries) rather than YAML-as-incidental-config, and that the honest fix is a second source. This is what measuring the candidates found.
second_source_investigated.registries_are_barren: PACKAGE REGISTRIES DO NOT CARRY YAML, measured across three: npm 15 top packages, 11,471 archive entries, **0** YAML files. crates.io 10 top crates, 1,225 entries, **6** (anyhow 2, itertools 4). PyPI sdists 10 top packages, 22,152 entries, **165** — of which 162 are numpy alone. 171 YAML files from 35 packages, 96% from one. The cause is structural rather than incidental: publishing strips exactly the files YAML lives in. `.npmignore` and package.json `files` drop `.github/`, cargo and sdists mostly do the same. So the obvious second source — reuse `npm::rank`, which is already generic and would have been a five-line change — is not viable, and that is a measured negative rather than an untried idea.
second_source_investigated.what_would_work: GitHub repositories in OTHER languages, which `github::rank(LangName::Yaml, "<host language>", k)` already supports without new code: the YAML is there because the repository is a project, not a package. Measured on the top 3 repos each for Go, Python and TypeScript: 874 YAML files from 9 repositories, against 216 MB of tarballs. That is roughly an order of magnitude more bandwidth per admitted file than the YAML-primary corpus (26,634 files from 100 repositories), and it is heavily skewed — 698 of the 874 come from one repository. So it is a real second population, worth adding when someone wants the incidental-config distribution specifically, and not worth switching to blind.
second_source_investigated.conclusion: The GitHub YAML-primary source stands, and now stands on a measurement rather than on the absence of an alternative.

current.headline: ZERO GRAMMAR GAPS and ONE accepts-invalid. Both remaining sweep failures are corpus noise the oracle rejects too. Everything below `ranked_corpus` is the history that got here and is deliberately NOT rewritten in place: it is patch 0003's before-picture.
current.measured_on: the ranked corpus at 26,636 files, and yaml/yaml-test-suite data-2022-01-17 at 402 cases. The two populations answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other: the sweep found 0003 and cannot see 0004-0006 at all, and the suite found 0004-0007 and cannot see a 32k-line CRD bundle.
current.what_is_left: ONE: suite case QLJ7, a tag shorthand `!prefix!` declared by a %TAG directive in the first document and used in later ones. js-yaml's reason is 'undeclared tag handle', which is NAME RESOLUTION and not syntax — it needs a per-document symbol table of declared handles, which a tree-sitter grammar has no place holding. Left unfixed deliberately rather than left unnoticed. The sweep side is exhausted: it can only ever find rejects-valid and there is nothing left to find.

ranked_corpus.what: The real corpus: top 100 GitHub repositories classified as YAML, fetched via `treebank fetch --lang yaml --limit 100`. 26,634 admitted files, 211 MB extracted. MEASURED AT THE PINNED SHA WITH THE TWO PACKAGING PATCHES ONLY — i.e. BEFORE patch 0003. It is kept as the measurement that found the row overflow and as 0003's before-picture; `corpus.sweep_upstream` / `corpus.sweep_patched` hold the controlled before/after on the corpus as it stood when 0003 landed, and `sweep.current` is where the grammar is now.
ranked_corpus.headline: 26,629 of 26,634 (99.98%) BEFORE patch 0003. ALL FOUR GAPS WERE ONE BUG — the int16 row overflow below. Truncating each of the four to exactly 32,768 lines made it parse clean, which is how one root cause was told from four coincidences. Patch 0003 fixed it and took this corpus to zero gaps, as predicted here; see `sweep.current`.
ranked_corpus.gap_files_detail: 72,060 / 49,299 / 49,054 / 35,649 lines — kuberay operator resources, argoproj.io_workflows.yaml, kserve-crds.yaml, a kubeflow manifest set. Generated Kubernetes CRD bundles, which is exactly the population predicted when the bug was diagnosed on a 40,011-line prometheus rules file. All four are fixed by patch 0003 and parse clean.
ranked_corpus.noise_file: open-education-api/specification ooapiv6.yaml, 25,567 lines — under the ceiling, ERROR at any truncation, and rejected by the oracle. Genuinely invalid, correctly booked as noise.
ranked_corpus.admit_drop: 35,017 YAML files are present in the 100 archives and 26,634 were admitted: classify()+admit() dropped 8,383 (23.9%), almost all bare `{{ }}` templates. Verified on the admitted corpus rather than assumed: 0 files carrying a bare `{{` action, 0 Jinja `{% %}`, 0 NUL-bearing — and 293 files whose only `{{` is a GitHub Actions `${{ }}`, correctly kept. The `$` lookbehind is what keeps those 293.
ranked_corpus.issue: https://github.com/PowderworksCode/treebank/issues/58, CLOSED by patch 0003; raised upstream at https://github.com/tree-sitter-grammars/tree-sitter-yaml/issues/49, which is still open and which we are not pursuing — the fix is carried as a local patch.

what_the_oracle_choice_costs.summary: THE ONE PLACE THE POSITION CHANGES THE ANSWER ON REAL DATA, measured. Over all 26,634 files the oracle rejects 7. The grammar rejects 1 of those (noise) and ACCEPTS the other 6 — but libyaml and go-yaml call all 6 of those VALID. So `grammar accepts-invalid = 6` under this oracle and would be 0 under either alternative.
what_the_oracle_choice_costs.the_construct: All 6 are one class: a multi-line flow collection as a block mapping value whose continuation and closing bracket sit at the SAME indentation as the key, e.g. `daj_util_objects: [` … `]` with the `]` in the key's column. js-yaml calls it "deficient indentation"; YAML 1.2.2 requires flow content nested in a block context to be indented past the parent, so js-yaml appears to be right and the other two lenient. It is a common shape because it is what pasted JSON looks like.
what_the_oracle_choice_costs.agreement_on_real_data: js-yaml, libyaml and go-yaml agree on 26,628 of 26,634 files (99.98%). The 67-of-402 disagreement the suite shows is a hard-tail phenomenon; on real YAML the choice of oracle moves 0.023% of verdicts. Both numbers are true and neither is quotable without the other.
what_the_oracle_choice_costs.consequence: `gap_files` is unaffected — all four gaps are files every parser calls valid — so the headline number does not depend on the position. What depends on it is the accepts-invalid count, which is the number a future patch would be judged against.

sweep.grammar_at_pinned_sha: 3217 measurement-corpus files, no admit() filter: 3114 clean, 103 ERROR. With admit() applied (2178 files): 4 ERROR, of which 3 are also rejected by the oracle (noise) and ONE is a gap. AT THE PINNED SHA, i.e. before patch 0003; that one gap is the row overflow and 0003 closes it.

the_one_gap.verdict: valid per js-yaml, libyaml AND go-yaml; ERROR per the grammar, spanning [0,0]-[32767,53]
the_one_gap.diagnosis: NOT a YAML construct — an integer overflow. At the pinned sha `src/scanner.c` kept ALL of its position state in `int16_t` (`row`, `col`, `blk_imp_row`, `blk_imp_col`, `blk_imp_tab`, and the two indent stacks). At row 32768 `row` wrapped negative and every indentation comparison after it was wrong, so the rest of the file became one ERROR node.
the_one_gap.minimal_repro: 32769 lines of `k<N>: <N>`. Bisected exactly: 32768 lines parse clean, 32769 do not, and 2**15 = 32768. A 200 KB single-line file parses clean, so it is rows and not bytes.
the_one_gap.scope: Any YAML document over 32768 lines, which is a normal size for generated manifests, CRD bundles and rule files.
the_one_gap.fixed_by: patch 0003, which widens `row`, `blk_imp_row`, the `cur_row`/`end_row` temporaries and the `bgn_row` local to `int32_t`, and orders serialize/deserialize so the two persistent 32-bit fields come first and every field stays naturally aligned (header 10 -> 14 bytes). The indent stacks are untouched, so the nesting depth that fits in TREE_SITTER_SERIALIZATION_BUFFER_SIZE is unchanged. THE COLUMNS ARE STILL int16_t AND WOULD WRAP THE SAME WAY PAST COLUMN 32767 — not fixed because no file in either corpus demonstrates it and fixing it properly means widening the two indent STACKS, which are serialized per indent level against a fixed buffer and would halve that depth. See patch 0003's `remaining_gaps_note`.

grammar_accepts_invalid.note: ONE: yaml-test-suite QLJ7 only, and it is out of scope by kind rather than by effort — see `sweep.current.what_is_left`. Patches 0004-0007 closed SF5V, QB6E, DK95/01, Y79Y/000 and S98Z, and all five now sit in test/negative, where the ledger previously said they could not go without being 'a to-do disguised as a test'. They are no longer to-dos.
grammar_accepts_invalid.history: This field read 7 and was measured at the pinned sha before patch 0003. Re-measured at the start of the 0004-0007 work it was 6, not 7: MUS6/01 (a %YAML directive after a document start) was already rejected. The stale entry is corrected rather than quietly overwritten, because a count that nobody re-runs is how this direction rots — the grammar had improved and the ledger had not noticed. 7 (claimed, pre-0003) -> 6 (measured) -> 1 (now).
grammar_accepts_invalid.measured_with: scripts-free: `treebank negative` over the suite's 94 expect-error cases, and the pinned CLI's `parse` over its 308 expect-valid cases. Both directions are scored on every change, because every one of 0004-0007 is a TIGHTENING and the failure mode of a tightening is rejects-valid.
